title: Ichalkaranji handloom & powerloom: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Ichalkaranji runs roughly 1 lakh looms weaving cotton, polyester and denim, and the trade began from handloom before moving to powerloom [1].** Cash comes from converting yarn into fabric and selling to traders; the loom owner's margin is the gap between yarn cost plus wage plus power and the trader's price. **Weaving is fixed-capital and working-capital intensive, and working capital is driven by inventory holding plus receivables [8][9].** So when a proposal lands, check the receivable days against the trader concentration; if one buyer is over half of sales, ask for the ledger and the buyer's payment record. ## What has broken now
**In May 2026 the looms were shut for eight days and the agitation turned violent, with a march on the local MLA's office [1][2].** That is a live cash-flow event, not background noise: a stopped loom earns nothing while wages, power and interest keep running. **The dispute is specifically between kharchiwala weavers, the Kolhapur District Powerloom Association and cloth traders, and was pushed to a collector-level meeting [1].** So when a job-work weaver proposes, ask whether his wage rate is settled in writing with his trader; if not, treat the account as unsecured trading exposure and size it accordingly. **Note the local sources are from March–May 2026 and predate today by about six months — collect from customer what has happened to the wage settlement since.**

## Where the growth is
**Maharashtra GST collections are running +8.6% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D], and all-India fabric output (NIC 13) is +13.1% YoY with +11.9% Apr-to-date [D]** — demand is there, and the state is pulling ahead. **The state textile budget carries 10% more allocation than last year with interest subsidy and energy concessions for textile projects [3].** Pursue the borrower who owns his looms, buys yarn directly, sells finished fabric on his own invoice, and can claim that interest subsidy. **Peer evidence from a listed weaver shows the model works when raw material is booked in advance: sales rose 42.04% to ₹111.36 crore and net profit 63.01% to ₹18.55 crore in the December 2025 quarter [6], and full-year net profit rose 60.72% to ₹64.61 crore [7].** Avoid the pure wage-dependent job-work unit with no yarn position and one trader buyer. ## How to grow safely
**Fund the yarn cycle, not the loom shed.** Structure as a cash-credit against hypothecated stock and receivables with a drawing power recalculated monthly, and keep term debt tenure long — rating methodology flags tenure as a key coverage driver [10]. **Take stock-and-receivable statements every month, GST returns every month, and power bills every month** (power is the tell on whether looms actually ran). Covenant that wage settlements be documented before any enhancement. **Keep leverage low: rating methodology ties low leverage directly to financial flexibility in a downturn [10].**

## Early warning signs
- **Loom-hours from power bills fall two months running (monthly) → freeze drawing power and visit the unit.**
- **Any fresh strike or collector-level wage meeting reported locally (weekly) → stop fresh sanctions to job-work accounts until it resolves [1].**
- **Receivable days stretch beyond the sanctioned cycle or one buyer crosses half of sales (monthly) → ask for the buyer's payment proof and reprice.**
- **GST turnover dips below the stock statement's implied sales (monthly) → call the account and inspect godown stock.**

turnover below implied sales -> inspect godown, call account
one buyer over half of sales -> demand payment proof, reprice
subsidy not credited -> check eligibility file before renewal [3]
